headline: Apple Teams Up With OpenEvidence to Study How People Use AI for Health Questions

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Apple made a new app to learn how people ask computers about health. The app lets people type questions about being sick or staying healthy, just like how some people ask chatbots questions. But this app only gives answers that come from real doctor science, like medical magazines that doctors trust. Apple is working with a company called OpenEvidence to build this app. They want up to 200,000 people in the United States to try it for about a year. People need an iPhone and must be over 21 years old to join. Users can also share things like their heart rate or sleep from their Apple Watch so the app can give better answers. The app can even help someone get ready for a doctor visit. Apple says they will keep people's information private and will erase it quickly. They are not using this information to teach other computer programs. Apple wants to learn if this kind of health help is actually useful for people, before deciding if they should add it to iPhones everywhere.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Many companies like OpenAI and Anthropic already let people ask their chatbots about health problems. Apple wants to try something a little different. Instead of releasing a health chatbot right away, Apple is running a big science study first, to understand how people actually use AI when they have health questions. Apple teamed up with a healthcare AI company called OpenEvidence to build a new app just for this study. People who join can ask questions about their health, and the app answers using trusted medical sources, like big medical journals doctors read. The app tries to explain things in a simple way anyone can understand. Up to 200,000 adults in the U.S. can join, and the study will run for more than a year. Users can connect their health data, like sleep or heart rate, from their iPhone or Apple Watch to get more personal suggestions. The app can also help someone figure out what to ask their doctor. Apple promises that all personal data is kept anonymous and safe, and that the questions and answers get deleted after only 24 hours. This matters because millions of people already ask AI chatbots about health every week, and experts want to make sure the advice is safe, accurate, and actually helpful rather than confusing or wrong.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Artificial intelligence chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude have become popular tools for people searching for quick answers to health questions, but there's growing concern over whether AI-generated medical advice is accurate or safe. Instead of jumping straight into offering its own AI health chatbot, Apple is taking a research-first approach. The company partnered with OpenEvidence, a healthcare-focused AI company, to create a new study app that explores how people actually interact with AI when asking about their health. To participate, users must be over 21, live in the U.S., and own a fairly recent iPhone running the newest software with a feature called Apple Intelligence turned on. Apple hopes to gather feedback from as many as 200,000 participants over more than a year. The app answers health questions using information backed by respected medical research, including journals like The New England Journal of Medicine and Nature, rather than relying on general internet information. After getting an answer, users can rate how helpful or accurate it was, and they'll also answer monthly survey questions about their experience. People can choose to connect personal health data, such as resting heart rate, activity levels, or lab results, so the app can give more personalized guidance, and even help someone prepare smart questions before a doctor's appointment. Apple states that all collected information is made anonymous and sent to a secure outside cloud service, and importantly, it will not be used to train AI systems. OpenEvidence also deletes each question and answer within 24 hours, which is meant to protect user privacy. This study matters because AI-driven health questions are already incredibly common — OpenAI reported earlier this year that people ask over 300 million health-related questions every week. By carefully studying how people understand and trust AI health answers before fully launching a product, Apple seems to be trying to build something more responsible and reliable, rather than rushing out a feature that could potentially spread confusing or incorrect medical information.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: As AI chatbots from companies like OpenAI and Anthropic increasingly answer medical questions for millions of users each week, concerns have grown about the reliability of AI-generated health advice. Rather than quickly releasing its own competing chatbot, Apple is approaching the issue cautiously by launching a structured research study. Partnering with OpenEvidence, a company specializing in clinically grounded AI for healthcare, Apple built a dedicated study app designed to examine how everyday people engage with, understand, and evaluate AI health information in real life. The study targets up to 200,000 U.S.-based adults over 21 who own an iPhone 15 or newer running the latest iOS software with Apple Intelligence enabled, and it is expected to run for more than a year. Inside the app, users can ask health-related questions similar to how they might use a general chatbot, but answers are intentionally grounded in peer-reviewed medical research from trusted sources such as The New England Journal of Medicine, JAMA, and Nature, rather than broad, unverified internet content. The app is designed to translate complex clinical information into simplified, accessible explanations, and participants are encouraged to rate the usefulness of answers and complete monthly surveys reflecting on their experience. To make the guidance more personal, users can optionally link HealthKit data such as sleep patterns, resting heart rate, physical activity, or lab results, allowing the app to tailor insights more precisely to an individual's health profile. The app can also help someone organize their thoughts and questions before a medical appointment, and it is built to direct users toward professional care when an issue seems serious. Apple has emphasized privacy protections throughout this process: all data is anonymized before being transmitted to a secure third-party cloud system, none of the information is used to train AI models, and OpenEvidence automatically deletes each interaction's query and response within 24 hours. Apple's Vice President of Health and Fitness, Dr. Sumbul Desai, described the effort as rooted in “scientific rigor and clinical grounding,” framing the study as a way to responsibly understand public trust in AI health tools before expanding further. This approach stands out in an industry often criticized for moving fast without fully testing real-world impact, and the results could eventually shape whether Apple integrates AI health answers directly into widely used tools like its Health app or Siri.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: The rapid rise of AI chatbots capable of answering medical questions — OpenAI reported more than 300 million health-related queries submitted weekly earlier this year — has intensified debate over how reliable, safe, and clinically sound such AI-generated advice truly is. While competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic have moved forward with embedding health-focused features directly into their chatbots, Apple is adopting a more deliberate, research-oriented strategy. The company has partnered with OpenEvidence, an AI firm specializing in clinically grounded medical information, to launch a dedicated study app rather than a fully public-facing product. The goal is explicitly investigative: to understand, through structured observation and feedback, how ordinary people interact with, interpret, and place trust in AI-generated health guidance within their daily lives. Eligible participants must be U.S. residents over the age of 21, own an iPhone 15 or later, and run iOS 26 with Apple Intelligence enabled — technical requirements that suggest Apple wants data from users already engaged with its broader AI ecosystem. The study is designed to scale significantly, inviting participation from up to 200,000 people over a period exceeding twelve months, a scope that could generate a substantial dataset on user behavior and perception. Functionally, the app resembles a conversational health assistant, but its answers are deliberately sourced from peer-reviewed, authoritative medical literature, including The New England Journal of Medicine, JAMA, and Nature, rather than the broader, often unverified corpus of information typical general-purpose chatbots draw from. Responses are intentionally simplified for accessibility, and users are prompted to rate the quality of answers while completing recurring monthly surveys, generating ongoing qualitative and quantitative feedback for researchers. A notable feature allows participants to voluntarily integrate HealthKit data, such as resting heart rate, physical activity levels, sleep metrics, or lab results, enabling more individualized and context-aware responses, while the app can also assist users in preparing informed questions ahead of clinical visits and direct them toward professional medical providers when symptoms appear serious. Privacy safeguards are emphasized throughout: data is anonymized prior to transmission to a secure third-party cloud infrastructure, explicitly excluded from AI model training, and automatically deleted by OpenEvidence within 24 hours of each query-response exchange. In a public statement, Apple's Vice President of Health and Fitness, Dr. Sumbul Desai, framed the initiative around “scientific rigor and clinical grounding,” positioning the study as foundational research intended to inform broader conversations about trust and effectiveness in health-related AI tools. This cautious, evidence-based approach contrasts with the competitive urgency seen elsewhere in the AI industry, and its outcomes may ultimately determine whether Apple integrates AI-driven health responses into mainstream products like the Health app or Siri, carrying significant implications for how millions of consumers access medical information in the future.

questions: If you could ask an AI chatbot about a health question, would you trust its answer as much as a doctor's? Why or why not?
Why do you think Apple wants to study how people use AI for health before actually launching the feature everywhere, instead of releasing it right away like other companies?
How might apps like this change the way people in your community learn about health, especially people who may not have easy access to doctors?
